https://www.walesonline.co.uk/news/news-.text: When I was younger "lucky" meant having no homework for the weekend, being allowed a bag of sweets, or winning my favourite video game. This year I was described as “lucky” after being poisoned. Without denying that being unharmed is fortunate to call it luck is to ignore the truth. Female safety while travelling is a topic rightly discussed frequently. For most young girls planning a trip it is a defining factor in every aspect of the holiday. From accommodation to packing lists, the goal of keeping young ladies safe is second nature. We carry pocket alarms as habitually as we carry house keys, having location services on is a necessity, and not being out alone at night is a rule drilled into us from a young age. Recently I embarked on the trip of a lifetime: interrailing across Europe. As a young female traveller safety was never far from my mind. I watched my drinks like a hawk and I planned my way home even before making evening plans. While in Prague we were drawn in by the exciting nightlife. We had made it through two nights – watching the sunrise before returning home – when disaster struck where we least expected it. Danger is often assumed to lie in clubs and bars but our “lucky” escape took place within the familiar surroundings of a pub. I still do not know who the culprit was but the evening turned sinister when I was overcome by overwhelming, paralysing exhaustion and had to be rushed back. As the night progressed so did my symptoms. What started as worrying fatigue turned into sickness-bug-like manifestations. Eventually I passed out in my bed safely, “luckily”, surrounded by 11 strangers. I had been spiked. People said I was lucky that day. I escaped with no physical harm, no lasting effects, and remained, overall, mentally unshaken – lucky me. Spiking is a widespread crime – one that sadly leaves women living in constant fear for their safety. I was not lucky. Luck is going out at night and not leaving early due to poisoning, luck is having my health completely in my control, and luck is not being unwell after a casual night with friends. Luck is me deciding when I want to go home. This so-called “luck” is not enough. Our responsibility to one another goes further: we must stop accepting near-misses as “good fortune” and instead prevent situations from ever reaching the point where we call them “lucky”, let alone letting them escalate into tragedies. When we frame escapes like this as luck we excuse the crime. We imply harm was inevitable and treat safety as a matter of chance. It is not. We have a duty to do better – to look out for each other, to report anything suspicious immediately, and to leave and seek help the moment something feels off or symptoms appear. Awareness, mutual care, and refusing to accept “getting away with it” as adequate protection – that is true safety. That is what should replace luck.

The Army veteran with more than 20 years of military experience spanning multiple deployments and companies — including as a paratrooper for the vaunted 82nd Airborne Division — did not retire his commitment to help others when he finished his military career. "His entire life was in service to others. Up until the very end, Sean was always thinking of others," Steven Rozina told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. Rozina, now the deputy chief operating officer for the nonprofit Independence Fund, which helps provide services and support to wounded veterans, met Lee when he too joined the nonprofit to continue his career of service. Rozina outlined Lee’s impressive post-military resume, which spanned three continents, in his efforts to continue helping people. "I think it was 2021, the fall of Afghanistan. Sean answered that call again. He helped evacuate thousands of our Afghan allies, people that worked with us, people that are our friends, that are still our friends today," Rozina explained.
